claim: Face processing has been studied extensively, but the dynamics of how face-selective cortical areas are engaged remains unclear.
source: Although face processing has been studied extensively, the dynamics of how face-selective cortical areas are engaged remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a motivation for the study.

claim: Processing of normal faces started in the posterior occipital areas and then proceeded to anterior regions.
source: Processing of normal faces started in the posterior occipital areas and then proceeded to anterior regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: The bottom-up processing sequence was observed even when internal facial features were misarranged.
source: This bottom-up processing sequence was also observed even when internal facial features were misarranged.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Processing of two-tone Mooney faces lacking explicit prototypical facial features engaged top-down projection from the right posterior fusiform face area to right occipital face area.
source: However, processing of two-tone Mooney faces lacking explicit prototypical facial features engaged top-down projection from the right posterior fusiform face area to right occipital face area.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Face-specific responses elicited by contextual cues alone emerged simultaneously in the right ventral face-selective regions.
source: Further, face-specific responses elicited by contextual cues alone emerged simultaneously in the right ventral face-selective regions, suggesting parallel contextual facilitation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: The processing of face information involves a distributed neural network of face-sensitive areas in the occipitotemporal cortex and beyond.
source: There is ample evidence to show that the processing of face information involves a distributed neural network of face-sensitive areas in the occipitotemporal cortex and beyond (Duchaine and Yovel, 2015; Haxby et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Three bilateral face-selective areas are considered as the core face-processing system: Occipital Face Area (OFA), Fusiform Face Area (FFA), and a face-sensitive area in the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS).
source: Three bilateral face-selective areas are considered as the core face-processing system, defined in functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) studies as regions showing significantly higher response to faces than objects, which are Occipital Face Area (OFA) in the inferior occipital gyrus (Gauthier et al., 2000; Haxby et al., 1999), Fusiform Face Area (FFA) in the fusiform gyrus (Kanwisher et al., 1997; Grill-Spector et al., 2004) and a face-sensitive area in the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) (Hoffman and Haxby, 2000; Puce et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous fMRI studies.

claim: A number of face patches have been identified in macaque monkeys along the superior temporal sulcus.
source: Similarly, a number of so-called face patches have been identified in macaque monkeys along the superior temporal sulcus (Tsao et al., 2003; Tsao et al., 2006; Tsao et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in macaque monkeys.

claim: Hierarchical models postulate that face specific processes are initiated in the OFA based on local facial features, then the information is forwarded to higher level regions, such as FFA, for holistic processing.
source: Hierarchical models postulate that face specific processes are initiated in the OFA based on local facial features, then the information is forwarded to higher level regions, such as FFA, for holistic processing (Haxby et al., 2000; Fairhall and Ishai, 2007; Liu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a description of existing hierarchical models supported by citations.

claim: Patients with damaged OFA can still show FFA activation to faces.
source: However, it has been challenged by results from studies in which patients with damaged OFA can still showed FFA activation to faces (Rossion et al., 2003; Steeves et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to patient studies.

claim: During the perception of faces with minimal local facial features, FFA could still show face-preferential activation without face-selective inputs from OFA.
source: Further, it was reported that during the perception of faces with minimal local facial features, FFA could still show face-preferential activation without face-selective inputs from OFA (Rossion et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A non-hierarchical model was proposed postulating that face detection is initiated at the FFA followed by a fine analysis in the OFA.
source: Thus a non-hierarchical model was proposed postulating that face detection is initiated at the FFA followed by a fine analysis in the OFA (Rossion et al., 2011; Gentile et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of an alternative model supported by citations.

claim: Right OFA (rOFA) and right posterior FFA (rpFFA) were activated very close in time, peaking around 120 ms.
source: Right OFA (rOFA) and right posterior FFA (rpFFA) were activated very close in time, peaking around 120 ms, while right anterior FFA (raFFA) reached its peak at about 150 ms.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section of the abstract.

claim: Right anterior FFA (raFFA) reached its peak at about 150 ms.
source: Right OFA (rOFA) and right posterior FFA (rpFFA) were activated very close in time, peaking around 120 ms, while right anterior FFA (raFFA) reached its peak at about 150 ms.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section of the abstract.

claim: The right pSTS (rpSTS) showed a weaker and temporally more variable response, participating in face processing within a time window from 130 to 180 ms.
source: The right pSTS (rpSTS) in the dorsal pathway showed a weaker and temporally more variable response, participating in face processing within a time window from 130 to 180 ms.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section of the abstract.

claim: According to the predictive coding theory, face prediction created at FFA based on impoverished information of Mooney faces and prior knowledge is poorly matched with the input representation at OFA due to the lack of explicit local facial features.
source: According to the predictive coding theory (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Murray et al., 2004; Mumford, 1992), face prediction created at FFA based on impoverished information of Mooney faces and prior knowledge is poorly matched with the input representation at OFA due to the lack of explicit local facial features.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on predictive coding theory, supported by citations.

claim: The activity in OFA, representing 'residual error' between top-down prediction and bottom-up input, is expected to increase subsequently when processing Mooney faces.
source: The activity in OFA, representing 'residual error' between top-down prediction and bottom-up input, is then expected to increase subsequently.
evidence: This is a prediction based on predictive coding theory.

claim: rOFA was activated later than rpFFA when processing Mooney faces.
source: Consistent with this model, rOFA was activated later than rpFFA, and rpFFA exerted extensive directional influence onto rOFA when processing Mooney faces, suggesting a cortical analysis dominated by rpFFA to rOFA projection.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section of the abstract.

claim: rpFFA exerted extensive directional influence onto rOFA when processing Mooney faces.
source: Consistent with this model, rOFA was activated later than rpFFA, and rpFFA exerted extensive directional influence onto rOFA when processing Mooney faces, suggesting a cortical analysis dominated by rpFFA to rOFA projection.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section of the abstract.

claim: When explicit internal facial features were available but misarranged within a normal face contour, a temporal pattern similar to that of normal faces was observed.
source: However, when ﻿explicit internal facial features were available but misarranged within a normal face contour, a temporal pattern similar to that of normal faces was observed.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section of the abstract.

claim: When face-specific responses were driven by contextual cues alone with the internal face features entirely missing, rOFA, rpFFA and raFFA were activated somewhat late and almost simultaneously.
source: Finally, we further investigated the temporal dynamics when face-specific responses were driven by contextual cues alone with the internal face features entirely missing (Cox et al., 2004). In this case, rOFA, rpFFA and raFFA were activated somewhat late and almost simultaneously, corresponding to contextual modulation that parallelly facilitated the processing of the core face-processing network.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section of the abstract, with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Subjects were presented with famous faces and familiar objects and instructed to perform a simple classification task (face or object) while their brain activity was recorded using MEG.
source: Subjects were presented with famous faces and familiar objects and instructed to perform a simple classification task (face or object) while their brain activity was recorded using MEG.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Each subject underwent both fMRI and MEG measurements.
source: Since each subject underwent both fMRI and MEG measurements, we could compare the face-selective regions defined by fMRI with the reconstructed MEG signals evoked by faces in the source space.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Face-selective regions in the occipitotemporal cortex were localized with fMRI contrasting responses to faces with that to objects.
source: Subjects' face-selective regions in the occipitotemporal cortex were localized with fMRI contrasting responses to faces with that to objects.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: MEG signals at different time points were reconstructed in the source space by computing LCMV beamformer solution on evoked data after preprocessing.
source: MEG signals at different time points were reconstructed in the source space by computing LCMV beamformer solution on evoked data after preprocessing (Van Veen et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method, supported by a citation.

claim: Face response areas identified by MEG are highly consistent with that defined by fMRI.
source: Similar spatiotemporal patterns of activation could be seen across the 13 subjects tested. These results show that face response areas identified by MEG are highly consistent with that defined by fMRI, thus it is a reasonable approach to extract the MEG time courses based on fMRI-guided region of interest (ROI).
evidence: This is a finding based on the comparison of MEG and fMRI data.

claim: Face images induced stronger responses compared to objects in face-selective areas, especially for the right hemisphere.
source: Face images induced stronger responses compared to objects in face-selective areas, especially for the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of MEG time courses.

claim: In the right hemisphere, face-evoked responses emerged earlier in the posterior areas than in the anterior areas, with peak responses occurring at 116 ± 6 ms, 125 ± 5 ms and 150 ± 10 ms for rOFA, rpFFA and raFFA, respectively.
source: In the right hemisphere, face-evoked responses emerged earlier in the posterior areas than in the anterior areas, the peak responses occurred at 116 ± 6 ms, 125 ± 5 ms and 150 ± 10 ms for rOFA, rpFFA and raFFA, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analysis of MEG time courses.

claim: There is no significant difference between rOFA and rpFFA peak response timing (t12 = 1.57, p=0.43, Bonferroni corrected).
source: Although there is no significant difference between rOFA and rpFFA (t12 = 1.57, p=0.43, Bonferroni corrected), the peak response timing of raFFA is significantly delayed compared with rpFFA (t11 = 3.21, p=0.025, Bonferroni corrected), suggesting a bottom-up process.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of MEG time courses.

claim: The peak response timing of raFFA is significantly delayed compared with rpFFA (t11 = 3.21, p=0.025, Bonferroni corrected), suggesting a bottom-up process.
source: Although there is no significant difference between rOFA and rpFFA (t12 = 1.57, p=0.43, Bonferroni corrected), the peak response timing of raFFA is significantly delayed compared with rpFFA (t11 = 3.21, p=0.025, Bonferroni corrected), suggesting a bottom-up process.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of MEG time courses, with an interpretation.

claim: OFA reached its peak response earlier than pFFA in the left hemisphere (lOFA:122 ± 5 ms, lpFFA:126 ± 6 ms), although this trend is not statistically significant (t11 = 0.64, p>0.05, Bonferroni corrected).
source: Similarly, OFA reached its peak response earlier than pFFA in the left hemisphere (lOFA:122 ± 5 ms, lpFFA:126 ± 6 ms), although this trend is not statistically significant (t11 = 0.64, p>0.05, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of MEG time courses.

claim: Dorsal face-selective region pSTS showed weaker and temporally broader responses, involved in face processing roughly from 130 to 180 ms.
source: In addition, dorsal face-selective region pSTS showed weaker and temporally broader responses, involved in face processing roughly from 130 to 180 ms.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of MEG time courses.

claim: The sequential progression from posterior to anterior regions along the ventral occipitotemporal cortex, especially the significantly delayed activation of raFFA, indicates a bottom-up hierarchical functional structure of the ventral face pathway.
source: The sequential progression from posterior to anterior regions along the ventral occipitotemporal cortex, especially the significantly delayed activation of raFFA, indicates a bottom-up hierarchical functional structure of the ventral face pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Unfamiliar face images showed essentially similar hierarchical dynamic sequences of face processing regardless of face familiarity.
source: In addition to famous faces, we also presented unfamiliar faces to subjects and analyzed the data in the same way. Results showed essentially similar hierarchical dynamic sequences of face processing regardless of face familiarity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of unfamiliar face data, with reference to a figure.

claim: Subjects could perceive at least 90% of the Mooney images as faces.
source: Verbal survey after the MEG experiment indicated that subjects could perceive at least 90% of the Mooney images as faces.
evidence: This is a finding from a verbal survey conducted after the experiment.

claim: In all face-selective areas except rOFA, similar peak latencies were observed during the perception of normal and Mooney faces.
source: In all face-selective areas except rOFA, similar peak latencies were observed during the perception of normal and Mooney faces.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of Mooney face data.

claim: Mooney face elicited a response with significantly longer latency in rOFA than normal face (paired t test, t23 = 4.009, p=0.001).
source: ﻿ Strikingly, Mooney face elicited a response with significantly longer latency in rOFA than normal face (paired t test, t23 = 4.009, p=0.001) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of Mooney face data, with reference to a figure.

claim: When processing Mooney faces, rOFA was engaged significantly later than rpFFA (rOFA:144 ± 8 ms, rpFFA: 117 ± 8 ms. Paired permutation test p=0.02. Bonferroni corrected).
source: However, when processing Mooney faces, rOFA was engaged significantly later than rpFFA (rOFA:144 ± 8 ms, rpFFA: 117 ± 8 ms. Paired permutation test p=0.02. Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of Mooney face data.

claim: The response curve of rOFA was temporally shifted to a later point while the temporal characteristics of rpFFA was not much different from its response to normal faces when processing Mooney faces.
source: The response curve of rOFA was temporally shifted to a later point while the temporal characteristics of rpFFA was not much different from its response to normal faces (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of Mooney face data, with reference to a figure.

claim: There were much more extensive directed influences from pFFA to OFA during the processing of Mooney than normal faces.
source: There were much more extensive directed influences from pFFA to OFA during the processing of Mooney than normal faces.
evidence: This is a finding from Granger causality analysis.

claim: rpFFA influenced rOFA in Mooney face condition ﻿continuously from 75 to 170 ms, which was more sparsely observed in normal face condition.
source: In particular, rpFFA influenced rOFA in Mooney face condition ﻿continuously from 75 to 170 ms, which was more sparsely observed in normal face condition.
evidence: This is a finding from Granger causality analysis.

claim: Compared with processing of normal faces, the cortical processing of Mooney faces is more dominated by the top-down rpFFA to rOFA projection.
source: Thus response time courses and Granger causality analysis together show that, compared with processing of normal faces, the cortical processing of Mooney faces is more dominated by the top-down rpFFA to rOFA projection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from time course and Granger causality analysis.

claim: The rOFA, rpFFA and raFFA were activated sequentially when processing face-like stimuli with misarranged internal features (rOFA: 132 ± 7 ms, rpFFA: 133 ± 5 ms, raFFA: 169 ± 12 ms).
source: Results show that the rOFA, rpFFA and raFFA were activated sequentially (rOFA: 132 ± 7 ms, rpFFA: 133 ± 5 ms, raFFA: 169 ± 12 ms. Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of distorted face data, with reference to a figure.

claim: Compared with the responses to normal faces, the activations in the rOFA and rpFFA were somewhat delayed in the case of the distorted faces.
source: Compared with the responses to normal faces, the activations in the rOFA and rpFFA were somewhat delayed in the case of the distorted faces.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of distorted face data.

claim: Unlike the Mooney faces, the distorted faces still engaged the OFA earlier than the FFA, presumably because of the explicitly available local facial features.
source: However, unlike the Mooney faces, the distorted faces still engaged the OFA earlier than the FFA, presumably because of the explicitly available local facial features.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of distorted face data, with an interpretation.

claim: While the dominant signals are consistent with a feedforward processing from OFA to FFA for distorted faces, there was a hint of a predictive error signal, possibly related to the misarranged spatial configurations, that produced a low activity in rOFA at a later stage.
source: While the dominant signals are consistent with a feedforward processing from OFA to FFA, there was a hint of a predictive error signal, possibly related to the misarranged spatial configurations, that produced a low activity in rOFA at a later stage.

claim: Previous studies showed that face-specific responses could be elicited by contextual body cues.
source: In real life, facial features are not always available. Previous studies showed that face-specific responses could be elicited by contextual body cues (Cox et al., 2004; Chen and Whitney, 2019; Martinez, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activation in rOFA, rpFFA and raFFA were significantly higher for the condition in which faces were clearly implied due to the contextual cues compared to the condition when objects were presented.
source: Activation in rOFA, rpFFA and raFFA were significantly higher for the condition in which faces were clearly implied due to the contextual cues compared to the condition when objects were presented (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of contextual cue data, with reference to a figure.

claim: When ﻿contextual cues were misarranged so that faces were not strongly implied, only the rOFA showed stronger activation than objects at a late stage.
source: However, when ﻿contextual cues were misarranged so that faces were not strongly implied, only the rOFA showed stronger activation than objects at a late stage (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of contextual cue data, with reference to a figure.

claim: During the perception of 'faces' generated from contextual cues alone, the rOFA, rpFFA and raFFA were all engaged at about the same and relatively late time (rOFA: 149 ± 12 ms, rpFFA: 149 ± 14 ms, raFFA: 155 ± 11 ms) rather than activated sequentially.
source: Furthermore, peak latency analysis revealed that during the perception of 'faces' generated from contextual cues alone, the rOFA, rpFFA and raFFA were all engaged at about the same and relatively late time (rOFA: 149 ± 12 ms, rpFFA: 149 ± 14 ms, raFFA: 155 ± 11 ms) rather than activated sequentially (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of contextual cue data, with reference to a figure.

claim: When the presence of a face was facilitated by external cues alone, the evoked responses in the core face-processing network emerged slowly and almost simultaneously.
source: Thus when the presence of a face was facilitated by external cues alone, the evoked responses in the core face-processing network emerged slowly and almost simultaneously.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from contextual cue data.

claim: The results systematically revealed an intricately detailed dynamic picture of face information processing.
source: Using a combined fMRI and MEG source localization approach, our results systematically revealed an intricately detailed dynamic picture of face information processing.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the overall findings.

claim: Within the ventral occipitotemporal face processing network, normal faces were processed mainly in a bottom-up manner through the hierarchical pathway where input information was processed sequentially from posterior to anterior ventral temporal cortex.
source: Within the ventral occipitotemporal face processing network, normal faces were processed mainly in a bottom-up manner through the hierarchical pathway where input information was processed sequentially from posterior to anterior ventral temporal cortex.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings for normal faces.

claim: During the processing of Mooney faces in the absence of prototypical facial features, top-down modulation was more prominent in which the dominant information flow was from the rpFFA to rOFA.
source: In contrast, during the processing of Mooney faces in the absence of prototypical facial features, top-down modulation was more prominent in which the dominant information flow was from the rpFFA to rOFA.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings for Mooney faces.

claim: Face-specific responses from contextual cues alone were evoked late and simultaneously across the rOFA, rpFFA and raFFA, suggesting that contextual facilitation acted parallelly on the core face-processing network.
source: Moreover, face-specific responses from contextual cues alone were evoked late and simultaneously across the rOFA, rpFFA and raFFA, suggesting that contextual facilitation acted parallelly on the core face-processing network.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings for contextual cues, with an interpretation.

claim: These results advance our understanding of the hierarchical and non-hierarchical models of face perception, especially underscoring the stimulus- and context-dependent nature of the processing sequences.
source: These results advance our understanding of the hierarchical and non-hierarchical models of face perception, especially underscoring the stimulus- and context-dependent nature of the processing sequences.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the implications of the findings.

source: During the perception of 2-tone Mooney faces, it is necessary to discount shadows and recover 3D surface structure from 2D images (Grützner et al., 2010).

source: Interestingly, only familiar objects, like faces, can be interpreted to be volumetric easily from 2-tone representations (Moore and Cavanagh, 1998; Hegde et al., 2007).

source: A top-down model emphasized the guidance of prior experience at higher levels (Cavanagh, 1991).

claim: Early visual processing is affected by high-level attributes in both human and monkey.
source: This model is supported by evidence from experiments showing that early visual processing is affected by high-level attributes in both human and monkey (Lee et al., 2002; Humphrey et al., 1997; Issa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The dynamics of MEG signals associated with processing Mooney faces, which highlights the top-down modulation, is consistent with the explanation based on predictive coding model.
source: As briefly mentioned in the results section, the dynamics of MEG signals associated with processing Mooney faces, which highlights the top-down modulation, is consistent with the explanation based on predictive coding model.

source: It proposed that hypotheses or predictions made at higher cortical areas are compared with, through feedback, representations at lower areas to generate residual error, which is then forwarded to higher stages as 'neural activity' (Rao and Ballard, 1999; Murray et al., 2004; Friston, 2005; Friston, 2010).

source: Specifically, the face model/prediction is generated at the rpFFA based on the global configuration of Mooney faces using prior knowledge about 3D faces, illumination, and cast shadows.

claim: The prediction of expected facial features is then poorly matched with the input representation at the rOFA which lacks the explicit prototypical facial features due to the mixed illumination-invariant and illumination-dependent features, generating an increased signal at rOFA.
source: This prediction of expected facial features is then poorly matched with the input representation at the rOFA which lacks the explicit prototypical facial features due to the mixed illumination-invariant and illumination-dependent features, generating an increased signal at rOFA.

source: Thus, the dominant signal at the rOFA (residual) necessarily lags behind the signal at the rpFFA (hypothesis).

source: However, when processing normal faces or face with misarranged facial features, the prominent signal in the early stage of rOFA is mainly due to the strong feedforward input from early visual cortex as rOFA is robustly responsive to the clear facial components.

source: The prediction feedback from rpFFA would be consistent with representation at the rOFA in the case of the normal faces, resulting in little error signal; with the misarranged facial features, there was a hint of a late increase of rOFA signal, possibly indicating that the feedback signal could contain some spatial information as well.

claim: With the misarranged facial features, there was a hint of a late increase of rOFA signal, possibly indicating that the feedback signal could contain some spatial information as well.
source: The prediction feedback from rpFFA would be consistent with representation at the rOFA in the case of the normal faces, resulting in little error signal; with the misarranged facial features, there was a hint of a late increase of rOFA signal, possibly indicating that the feedback signal could contain some spatial information as well.

claim: The timing of face induced neural activation has been studied for a long time with various techniques, such as the combination of MEG and fMRI using representational similarities, MEG source localization and intracranial EEG.
source: The timing of face induced neural activation has been studied for a long time with various techniques, such as the combination of MEG and fMRI using representational similarities (Cichy et al., 2014; Cichy et al., 2016), MEG source localization and intracranial EEG (Kadipasaoglu et al., 2017; Keller et al., 2017; Ghuman et al., 2014).

source: An early MEG study suggested two stages (﻿early categorization and ﻿late identification) were involved in face processing (Liu et al., 2002).

claim: OFA is responsible for identifying facial parts while FFA for holistic configuration.
source: Combined with the fMRI observation that OFA is responsible for identifying facial parts while FFA for holistic configuration (Rotshtein et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2010; Pitcher et al., 2011b; Arcurio et al., 2012; Pitcher et al., 2007; Schiltz, 2010), OFA is expected to respond earlier than FFA.

claim: The results provide more precise and detailed timing information of the core face network under various stimulus and contextual conditions, ﻿especially the temporal relationship between rpFFA and raFFA.

source: Although when assembling into a whole face, facial features are processed holistically and the representation of internal features are influenced by external features (Andrews et al., 2010), eyes in isolation elicit a later but larger N170 (Bentin et al., 1996; Rossion and Jacques, 2011) and can drive face-selective neurons as well as full-face images (Issa and DiCarlo, 2012) in monkeys.
